title: Rate-tapered admission with memory-aware priority decay for surge resilience
creator: Asha Menon
description:
Problem statement:
Under recent production spikes (observed in us-west and eu regions) the admission controller's fixed micro-batch thresholds produce oscillatory behavior: sudden QPS surges exhaust GPU headroom and KV hot shards, causing repeated evictions, longer tail latencies, and occasional OOM throttles. Existing fast-evict heuristics are reactive and introduce a throughput cliff, hurting 95/99th latency and increasing cost from repeated cold loads.

Goal:
Design and ship a rate-tapered admission controller combined with a memory-aware priority-decay mechanism and a soft-KV-reclamation path that: (1) reduces oscillation during high QPS ramps, (2) preserves tail-latency SLOs for high-priority requests, and (3) reduces unnecessary GPU-to-host spills. Target: improve p95 latency under sustained 8k QPS synthetic surge by at least 30% and eliminate transient GPU OOMs observed in prior incidents.

Design summary (high level):
- Rate-tapered admission: instead of a single accept/reject threshold, admission probability is gradually reduced as short-term GPU headroom falls. The taper uses a tunable curve (sigmoid with a configurable knee) operating on a 1s sliding window of headroom metrics to avoid step changes at fixed thresholds.
- Memory-aware priority decay: requests carry a priority token (customer, route, or system). When headroom is constrained, low-priority tokens decay eligibility over a time window (exponential decay) making them progressively less likely to be admitted; this prevents low-priority floods from evicting KV entries that high-priority traffic relies on.
- Soft-KV reclamation: introduce a two-tier reclamation pipeline: (a) proactive warm eviction of stale prefixes into host-resident compressed shards (asynchronously) and (b) probabilistic microbatch trimming where we preferentially remove tail requests inside micro-batches with low estimated utility. Both operate under a budget to avoid sudden cache churn.
- Hotness-aware batching: admission controller consults a lightweight KV hotness heatmap (per-tenant, per-prefix) to prefer admission of requests that are likely to hit cached KV; if not, the controller penalizes admission probability to favor cache-friendly traffic.

Trade-offs and rationale:
- Smooth tapering reduces oscillation but can increase short-term token latency for some requests; priority decay mitigates this for critical traffic.
- Warm eviction to host memory trades CPU and host memory for GPU stability; we limit background transfers to maintain host NIC/PCIe budgets.
- Probabilistic trimming may drop low-utility tokens; this is configurable per-route and can be disabled for strict correctness workloads.

Implementation plan (milestones):
1) Prototype in simulator and local benchmark harness (done).
2) Implement admission curve + headroom signal in admission-controller binary; add config knobs and metrics (in review: PR #4582).
3) Implement priority token plumbing through request context and decay logic; unit tests added.
4) Integrate hotness heatmap (LRU + decaying counters), expose limited rollup to admission controller.
5) Soft-KV pipeline: async shard emitter and host-resident compressed store.
6) Canary rollout to dedicated cluster tier with synthetic surge generator and shadowing.

Progress updates (chronological):
- 2026-02-15: Kickoff. Confluence design doc created: https://redwood.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/INF/pages/Rate+Tapered+Admission+Design.
- 2026-02-20: Simulator results: under synthetic 8k sustained QPS with mixed priorities, taper+priority-decay reduced oscillation and eliminated transient OOMs in 18/20 runs. p95 improved from 420ms to 270ms in simulator.
- 2026-02-24: Initial admission-controller changes implemented; metrics exported (admission_probability, taper_knee, headroom_window_ms). PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/4582 (review pending).
- 2026-02-28: Priority token propagation implemented across gRPC boundary; added compatibility layer for legacy SDKs. Integration tests green.
- 2026-03-01: Hotness heatmap prototype hooked to admission controller; initial experiments show admission rate for cache-friendly routes rose ~15% leading to 6% lower overall GPU memory churn.
- 2026-03-03: Canary plan approved by SRE and PM. Preparing smoke tests and rollback criteria.

Testing and results so far:
- Unit/sim tests: deterministic replay harness validated decay curve stability across 200 synthetic traces.
- Local perf: sustained 8k QPS mixed-priority workload:
  * baseline (no taper): p95=420ms, transient OOMs observed ~1.2x per-minute
  * taper + priority-decay + warm-evict (sim): p95=270ms, no transient OOMs
  * taper + hotness filter (sim): reduced cache churn by 18%
- Resource costs: warm-evict increases host memory by ~1.1GB per GPU shard and background PCIe traffic by ~6-8MB/s on bursts; within current host budgets but needs monitoring.

Rollout plan and safety:
- Start with 10% traffic on canary dedicated cluster for 24h with synthetic surge injections and real traffic shadowing.
- SLOs to watch: p95 latency, OOM counts, KV eviction rate, host PCIe bandwidth utilization.
- Immediate rollback triggers: any OOMs after rollout, >20% increase in p95 for high-priority routes, or >40% increase in eviction rate.

Open questions / decisions needed:
- Default taper curve: sigmoid knee at 30% headroom vs linear taper? (Recommendation: sigmoid; reduces sensitivity to small metric noise.)
- Host warm-evict storage format: compressed shard format vs mmapped prefix store (trade CPU vs page fault behavior). POC currently uses compressed shards.
- Priority semantics for third-party tenants: should we expose a public SDK token for priority hints or gate via billing/entitlement? PM prefers entitlement-based approach for now.

Dependencies and related issues:
- Depends on: ["ENG-30210","ENG-33120"] for admission controller metric plumbing and headroom estimator.
- Related: ENG-21987 (KV admission scoring), ENG-80211 (observability - new metrics).
